b: As a player at a chess club in Bremen, it is almost a matter of honour to take an interest in the English Opening, which in Germany was also known as the “Bremen Opening” in honour of Carl Carls. What I particularly like about this opening is its flexibility, the various move orders and the possible transpositions into other openings.

The ChessBase catalogue includes several video courses dealing with the English Opening. Here I would like to give you an overview of the most important courses and share my personal assessments with you. First, here is a table summarising the courses discussed, which will then be presented individually:
ABC of the English Opening by Lorin D'Costa

Success in the English is based upon understanding the plans and ideas available within this interesting opening. The games in this DVD will provide with exactly that-the armoury to play the English Opening as white with confidence!

This course is particularly suitable for beginners who have had little or no experience with the English Opening. Although the author presents a more or less complete repertoire for White based on variations with 2.g3, the main emphasis is on explaining the strategic and positional ideas behind this opening.
All the important variations are discussed through 35 illustrative games. The course is supplemented by interactive test videos and a database containing further games.

Marin's English Love –
A complete repertoire after 1.c4 for White

The aim of these Dvd's is to build a repertoire after 1.c4 and 2.g3 for White. The first DVD includes the systems 1...e5, the Dutch and Indian setups. The second DVD includes the systems with 1...c5, 1...c6 and 1...e6.
Mihail Marin's two-volume course is the major “standard reference” for anyone looking for a comprehensive English Opening repertoire for White, also based on variations with 2.g3.
Volume 1 deals with systems arising after 1.c4 e5 as well as Dutch and Indian setups by Black. Volume 2 covers systems following 1...e6, 1...c6 and the Symmetrical Variation 1...c5.
The English Opening by Simon Williams

Simon Williams also presents a repertoire for White in his two-volume course. Unlike D´Costa and Marin, he recommends systems with 2.Nc3, in which the fianchetto of the king's bishop is often, though not always, omitted in favour of preparing the central advance d4. In keeping with his own playing style, his repertoire is rather aggressive and combative.

I have incorporated some of Simon Williams' variations into my own repertoire. The only recommendation with which I have not had good experiences is 4.d4 in the Four Knights Variation (1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6). Today, I would advise players who do not wish to play the main line with 4.g3 to consider systems with 4.e3 (my choice) or 4.e4 instead.
The English Opening - Tactics and Strategy Turbo by Mihail Marin

This course is a useful supplement to the repertoire courses for White. It consists entirely of interactive exercises that allow you to train and test your tactical and strategic knowledge in positions arising from the English Opening.
Reversed Sicilian Power - Win with 1.c4 e5! by Nico Zwirs

In this course, IM Nico Zwirs presents the Reversed Sicilian as a powerful and practical weapon for White
In this course, IM Nico Zwirs presents the Reversed Sicilian as a powerful and practical weapon for White. The core idea is simple: players who already play the Sicilian with Black can leverage their existing knowledge to build a dynamic and effective setup with White.
Free video sample: Introduction
Free video sample: 2.d3 Sidelines

The course by Dutch IM Nico Zwirs is aimed at players who enjoy playing the Sicilian Defence with Black and would also like to play “their” Sicilian variation (e.g. the Najdorf, Taimanov or Dragon) with White. He therefore concentrates on various systems following 1.c4 e5; other moves by Black are covered only briefly in an additional video.

In addition to the common moves 2.Nc3 and 2.g3, the author also examines modern variations such as 2.d3, e3 and a3. This also makes the course very useful for players who answer 1.c4 with e5 as Black and want to prepare for these variations.
Let us now turn to courses that present a repertoire “against” the English Opening:

A Complete Black Repertoire versus the English, 1...e5
by Nicholas Pert

1...e5 against the English is a theoretically sound response with good chances of equality or better in all variations, and in this video series I provide a complete Black repertoire based on this move.
English grandmaster and trainer Nicholas Pert presents a repertoire against the English Opening based on 1...e5.

The author relies on solid systems that have proved their worth in grandmaster practice, such as 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bb4 and 1.c4 e5 2.g3 c6. However, sidelines are also discussed in detail and, as usual, the author also examines the tactical and strategic characteristics of the resulting positions.
A Complete Black Repertoire against 1.Nf3 & 1.c4 by Robert Ris

This video course offers you a complete, clear repertoire for Black against the moves 1.Nf3 and 1.c4. The recommended variations are easy to learn and not difficult to remember, but also pose White serious challenges.

This course by Robert Ris is the second part of a two-volume series presenting a repertoire against 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4. Alongside a repertoire against the English Opening, we also get a repertoire against the Réti Opening, 1.Nf3. This can be very helpful, as the two openings feature many transpositions and frequently lead into one another.
Against the English Opening, the author recommends a kind of “Grand Prix Attack” familiar from the Sicilian Defence, but with colours reversed: a setup with e5, Nc6 and then f5.
In addition to the major video courses, there are also “60-minute” courses devoted to specific variations of the English Opening:
Kramnik-Shirov Counter Attack: Surpirse Weapon against English by Andrew Martin

I was not previously aware that the variation 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 was called the “Kramnik-Shirov Counter Attack”, and it is not particularly new either. Andrew Martin's new course offers a compact repertoire against one of the main continuations in the English Opening. In my own practical experience, too, the variation is perfectly playable.

3.Nd5 is the critical variation here, and the author covers it in considerable detail. Other continuations lead to positions reminiscent of the Rossolimo Variation of the Sicilian Defence and do not pose any particular opening problems for Black.

Another tip: Anyone looking for an additional, easy-to-learn variation for Black against 1.c4 e5 2.g3 could, for example, consider 2...d5 3.cxd5 Qxd5). This may look rather crude, but it is perfectly playable and reduces the preparation required for a repertoire against the English Opening to a minimum.
Adhiban Gambit against 1.c4 by Robert Ris
The variation Robert Ris calls the “Adhiban Gambit” arises after 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 e4?!

This is a new attempt to make 3...e4, followed by 4.Ng5 c6!, playable at least in games with shorter time controls. Previously, the main continuation after 4.Ng5 was the “Bellon Gambit”, arising after 4...b5. Fans of risky but interesting gambit variations will find plenty to enjoy here.
The ChessBase catalogue offers a good and sufficiently wide selection of courses for anyone wishing to play the English Opening with White or to face it with Black.
